title: The Secret Life of Bees
full_review:
"The Secret Life of Bees" (Fox Searchlight) is a beautifully produced adaptation of Sue Monk Kidd's best-seller set in South Carolina.

Dakota Fanning plays Lily Owens, a 14-year-old who, years earlier, had accidentally shot her mother to death, as the latter was packing her suitcase intending to leave Lily's violent father, T. Ray (Paul Bettany).

Now, years later, the lonely girl pines for her mother, and wonders whether her mother would have taken her away with her. The guilt-wracked Lily treasures the few keepsakes she has of her, including a faded label with the image of a black Madonna.

Lily lives under the stern and erratic dictates of the alcoholic T. Ray, who treats any infraction harshly, making the girl kneel on grits until her knees bleed.

It is 1964 and the beginning of the civil rights era, and their barely literate housekeeper, Rosaleen (Jennifer Hudson), has announced she plans to register to vote, but on her way to do so, accompanied by Lily, she's savagely beaten by bigots, and winds up in the hospital. Fearing a lynch mob, Lily insists they flee.

In a nearby town, Lily happens upon bottles of honey decorated with labels showing the black Madonna. When the shopkeeper informs her that the honey is produced by the nearby Boatwright sisters, Lily seeks out their Pepto Bismol-pink house and asks for shelter.

The eldest of the sisters, August Boatwright (Queen Latifah), runs the honey concern, assisted by uptight sister June (Alicia Keys), a music teacher who at first resents Lily and holds her own adoring beau (Nate Parker) at arm's length, and sweet but simple-minded May (Sophie Okonedo), still grieving for her twin sister who died long ago. The sisters revere a large statue of the black Madonna, in their living room, even holding religious services for the neighbors.

Lily becomes part of the family, apprenticing in the bee business, blissfully content with her new life, and feeling she is somehow fated to be there. And she ignores the subtle prejudice of the townspeople who wonder at a white teenager living with a black family. Some surprising revelations are in store, but not before some gut-wrenching tragedy, prompted by Lily's innocuous movie date with August's godson, Zach (Tristan Wilds). Writer-director Gina Prince-Bythewood elicits well-judged performances from the cast, with Latifah and Dakota particularly outstanding. Latifah just goes from strength to strength in each film, and this is one of her best roles, allowing her to convey strong maternal warmth and wisdom.

If Dakota is not the best child actor ever to grace the screen, you'll be hard pressed to think of anyone better when watching her amazingly nuanced and sensitive acting here, which tops even her impressive work in the otherwise misguided "Hounddog," which opened in September.

The compassionate, albeit at times melodramatic, story includes elements of forgiveness and redemption, and a strong affirmation of family. Bring Kleenex.

The film contains some profanity and crude language, racial epithets and violence, nonsexual child abuse, light underage sensuality, murder and suicide; it's acceptable for older teens The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
